definition: Something, such as a reward, that encourages a person to do something or to try harder.
example: The free bus pass gave commuters an incentive to leave their cars at home.
nuance: An incentive is an outside reward or benefit that encourages action, while a motive is the inner reason a person acts.
prompt: A bakery wants more customers to visit on its slow Monday mornings.
options: Half-price muffins on Mondays gave early risers an incentive to stop by.
Raising Monday prices sharply was an incentive that kept customers away.
The rude cashier's incentive remark upset a regular customer.
The bakery's biggest incentive was the new oven it bought for the kitchen last spring.
reasons: A discount is an outside reward that encourages people to come in.
Something that drives people off is a deterrent, the reverse of an incentive.
This confuses the noun with the look-alike adjective "insensitive."
Kitchen equipment that customers never see does not encourage anyone to visit.

practice.prompt: A school library hopes students will read more books over the summer.
options: A pizza party was the librarian's incentive for students who read ten books.
The incentive of late fees made students afraid to borrow any books at all.
The librarian incentive the students by posting a reading chart.
Her incentive for skipping the reading list was that she simply forgot about it.
reasons: A promised party is a reward that encourages students to keep reading.
A penalty that scares students away discourages reading, so it is not an incentive.
The word is a noun; the action of encouraging this way is "incentivize."
Forgetting is an accident, not a reward or benefit that pushes someone to act.
